note: Knock-ons of repealing, amending or restoring Acts, by dimension. Written for this atlas from the statutes themselves and the sources named; 'assumption' marks a number chosen for the model rather than taken from an official estimate. Effects on the simulator may only move existing fiscal and service levers. No law change creates new powers, and none can unlock measures that strip citizenship or residence by ethnicity or that enable sterilisation or eugenics.

repeal.text: Repeal removes the powers and duties the Act created. Bodies it set up, and secondary legislation made under it, fall unless a saving provision keeps them. Section 16 of the Interpretation Act 1978 preserves rights and liabilities that had already accrued.
No modelled fiscal effect. Use the simulator's levers for any spending or tax change that would follow.

amend.text: An amendment changes only the provisions it names. Draft it in the drafting workspace to set out exactly which sections change.

restore.text: Re-enacting a repealed Act revives it only as far as the new Act says. Later legislation that replaced it would also need amending to avoid two regimes covering the same ground.

acts.title: Equality Act 2010
acts.summary: The main anti-discrimination law in Great Britain. It covers nine protected characteristics in work, services, education and public functions, sets the public sector equality duty (s.149), and requires gender pay gap reporting. It replaced the Race Relations, Sex Discrimination, Equal Pay and Disability Discrimination Acts.

knock.text: Statutory protection against discrimination in employment, goods and services, housing and education would end in Great Britain. There would be no equal pay claims, no duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, and no public sector equality duty. Public authorities would still be bound by Article 14 of the ECHR through the Human Rights Act, but only when another Convention right is engaged, and only against the state, not private employers or traders.

Repeal does not authorise discrimination by the state. Removing anyone's citizenship or residence because of race or ethnicity would still breach the Human Rights Act and the UK's obligations under ICERD, which the UK ratified in 1969.

The UK–EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement commits the UK not to weaken labour and social protections in a way that affects trade or investment. Repeal would invite EU 'rebalancing' measures and dispute settlement. In Northern Ireland, Article 2 of the Windsor Framework bars any diminution of rights protected by the 1998 Agreement, which keeps several EU anti-discrimination directives in force there.
The UN CERD and CEDAW committees review UK compliance periodically. Repeal would be reported as a regression.

Small direct savings: the Equality and Human Rights Commission's grant (about £17m a year) and public bodies' equality duty work. Discrimination claims would fall, but employers would face uncertainty while courts worked out what remained. No lever is moved.

Disabled people would lose the right to reasonable adjustments. Women would lose the statutory route to equal pay. Ethnic minority, LGBT and older workers would lose protection from dismissal or refusal of service on those grounds. Evidence from before 1965, when discrimination in housing and work was lawful and widespread, suggests outcomes would worsen most for groups with the least bargaining power.

amend.label: Remove the public sector equality duty (s.149)

knock.text: Public bodies would no longer have to have 'due regard' to equality when they make decisions. Judicial reviews based on the duty would end. Discrimination itself would stay unlawful.
Saves some officer time on equality impact assessments. No official estimate exists, and the saving is likely small next to departmental budgets.
Less systematic attention to how cuts or reforms fall on disabled people and other groups. The 2013 government review found the duty's costs and benefits hard to measure.

amend.label: Commence the socio-economic duty (s.1) in England

knock.text: Section 1 requires public bodies to consider how to reduce inequalities from socio-economic disadvantage. It is in force in Scotland (since 2018) and Wales (since 2021), but has never been commenced in England.
This is a process duty: its effect depends on how bodies apply it. Reviews in Scotland found mixed implementation.

acts.title: Race Relations Act 1965
acts.summary: The first British law against racial discrimination, covering public places. It was repealed and replaced by the Race Relations Act 1976, which the Equality Act 2010 in turn replaced.

knock.text: Already superseded. Its protections exist, in wider form, in the Equality Act 2010. Restoring it would add nothing unless the Equality Act were repealed, and even then it covered only public places and had no enforcement through the courts.

acts.title: Race Relations Act 1968
acts.summary: Extended the ban on racial discrimination to housing, employment and services. It was repealed by the Race Relations Act 1976.

knock.text: Already superseded, in wider form, by the Equality Act 2010. Restoring it would only matter if the Equality Act were repealed.

acts.title: Race Relations Act 1976
acts.summary: Made direct and indirect racial discrimination unlawful and set up the Commission for Racial Equality. It was repealed by the Equality Act 2010, which restated its protections.

knock.text: Its content lives on in the Equality Act 2010. Restoring it alongside that Act would create two overlapping regimes. Restoring it after repealing the Equality Act would bring back race protection only.

acts.title: Race Relations (Amendment) Act 2000
acts.summary: Passed after the Macpherson report into Stephen Lawrence's murder. It brought the police within race discrimination law and created a race equality duty for public authorities, later folded into the public sector equality duty.

knock.text: Its substance is now in the Equality Act 2010, including the duties on the police and the public sector equality duty. Repealing this Act alone changes little.

acts.title: Race Relations (Remedies) Act 1994
acts.summary: Removed the cap on compensation for race discrimination. It was repealed in 2010, and the Equality Act keeps compensation uncapped.

acts.title: Sex Discrimination Act 1975
acts.summary: Outlawed sex discrimination in employment, education and services. It was replaced by the Equality Act 2010.

knock.text: Superseded by the Equality Act 2010.

acts.title: Equal Pay Act 1970
acts.summary: Gave women the right to equal pay for equal work. It was replaced by the equality of terms provisions in the Equality Act 2010.

knock.text: Superseded by the Equality Act 2010.

acts.title: Disability Discrimination Act 1995
acts.summary: Introduced disability discrimination law and the duty to make reasonable adjustments. In Great Britain it was replaced by the Equality Act 2010, but it still applies in Northern Ireland.

knock.text: In Great Britain it is already replaced. In Northern Ireland it is still the main disability discrimination law, so repeal would remove that protection there.
In Northern Ireland, Article 2 of the Windsor Framework bars any diminution of rights under the 1998 Agreement. Repeal there would be open to challenge.

acts.title: Human Rights Act 1998
acts.summary: Makes the rights in the European Convention on Human Rights enforceable in UK courts. It requires public authorities to act compatibly and courts to read legislation compatibly where possible, and lets higher courts declare an Act incompatible.

knock.text: The UK would remain bound by the Convention under international law. People would have to take cases to Strasbourg, as before 2000, which takes years. UK courts would lose the duty to read laws compatibly and the power to make declarations of incompatibility.

The devolution Acts separately require devolved law and ministers to comply with Convention rights: Scotland Act 1998 s.29 and s.57, Government of Wales Act 2006 s.108A, and Northern Ireland Act 1998 s.6 and s.24. Repealing the Human Rights Act does not remove those limits, and changing them would engage the Sewel convention.

Under the 1998 Belfast/Good Friday Agreement, the UK committed to incorporate the Convention into Northern Ireland law. The Trade and Cooperation Agreement's law-enforcement cooperation rests on respect for the Convention and can be terminated if the UK denounces it. Repealing the Human Rights Act is not denunciation, but the EU and Irish governments would treat it as a signal.
No material direct effect. There might be more Strasbourg judgments and compensation awards, which are small sums.
Fewer quick domestic remedies, for example in care homes, mental health detention, inquests (Article 2) and immigration cases (Article 8).

amend.label: Replace with a domestic bill of rights

knock.text: Depends on the drafting. The 2022 Bill of Rights Bill would have weakened the duty to read laws compatibly and limited positive obligations. It was withdrawn in 2023.
Smaller than outright repeal if the Convention is still given effect, but the Northern Ireland commitments still apply.

acts.title: Climate Change Act 2008
acts.summary: Sets the legally binding target of net zero emissions by 2050 (amended in 2019), five-year carbon budgets, and the Climate Change Committee.

knock.text: The net zero target, the carbon budgets and the Climate Change Committee would end. Judicial reviews of the government's delivery plans, such as the successful challenges in 2022 and 2024, would lose their basis.

The UK's Paris Agreement pledge would remain an international commitment, but the domestic legal backing for it would go. The UK wrote the first climate framework law, and repealing it would damage its standing in COP negotiations.
No direct saving, because net zero spending is set by policy, not by the Act. Investors would face more policy uncertainty, which can raise the cost of capital for low-carbon projects.
The impact depends on what replaces the policies the Act drives.

amend.label: Move the net zero target to 2060

knock.text: Carbon budgets would be reset. The Climate Change Committee would advise on the new path.
The UK would be seen as backsliding on its Paris commitments, and ambition levels are reviewed at every COP.

acts.title: Bank of England Act 1998
acts.summary: Gives the Bank of England operational independence over interest rates to meet the inflation target the Chancellor sets, through the Monetary Policy Committee.

knock.text: Monetary policy would return to the Treasury. The Monetary Policy Committee's statutory basis would end.

Investors would expect higher inflation and demand a premium to hold gilts. After the September 2022 mini-budget, long gilt yields rose by more than one percentage point within days. The model assumes a lasting 0.5 point rise in yields.
Central bank independence is standard among G7 economies and expected by the IMF. Ending it would be read as a move towards fiscal dominance.

acts.title: Budget Responsibility and National Audit Act 2011
acts.summary: Created the Office for Budget Responsibility, which produces the official economic and fiscal forecasts, and reformed the National Audit Office.

knock.text: Official forecasting would go back to the Treasury. The National Audit Office's governance provisions would also need re-enacting.

Markets would treat the loss of independent forecasts as weaker discipline. The model assumes a lasting 0.25 point rise in gilt yields. Bypassing the OBR was part of the September 2022 market reaction.

acts.title: Localism Act 2011
acts.summary: Among other things, it inserted the council tax referendum rules: councils must hold a local referendum to raise council tax above the government's limit.

knock.text: Councils could raise council tax freely. The model assumes, on average, 2 points a year more than the limit allows, with the money staying with councils.
Council tax is regressive against property values, which are still based on 1991 bands. Larger rises fall hardest on lower-income households in areas with low property values.

acts.title: Health and Care Act 2022
acts.summary: Abolished clinical commissioning groups, created 42 integrated care boards, merged NHS Improvement into NHS England, and loosened competition rules.

knock.text: Without replacement, commissioning would revert to the 2012 structures, which no longer exist on the ground. In practice a new reorganisation Act would be needed.
The Department of Health estimated the transition costs of the 2012 reorganisation at about £1.5bn. The model assumes £0.75bn a year for two years.
Reorganisations distract management for years. The evidence on the 2012 reforms finds disruption and little benefit.

acts.title: Health and Social Care Act 2012
acts.summary: The Lansley reforms. They created clinical commissioning groups and NHS England, and moved public health to councils. Much of the commissioning structure was replaced in 2022.

knock.text: Much of it was already replaced by the Health and Care Act 2022. Repealing what remains, including the public health functions moved to councils, would need replacement provisions.
No modelled effect beyond the reorganisation itself.

acts.title: Children and Families Act 2014
acts.summary: Part 3 created education, health and care plans (EHCPs) for children and young people with special educational needs up to age 25. Councils have a legal duty to secure the provision in a plan.

knock.text: The legal entitlement to the provision in an EHCP would end, and tribunal appeals would end with it. Over 600,000 children and young people have plans.

Demand-led high-needs costs, which drive council deficits, would become discretionary. The atlas models the deficit's growth as a parameter, so no lever moves. Change 'Growth in high-needs (SEND) deficits' in the simulator's Parameters to test it.
Families would lose an enforceable right. Councils would ration support, and parents with fewer resources would be least able to secure it.
Reduces post-19 placement costs. Over-19s are a small share of plans but some of the most expensive placements.
Young people aged 19 to 25 would lose support at the transition to adulthood.

acts.title: Housing Act 1996
acts.summary: Part 7 sets councils' homelessness duties. The main duty (s.193) requires them to secure accommodation for eligible households in priority need who are unintentionally homeless.

knock.text: Councils would no longer have to house families in priority need. Section 17 of the Children Act 1989 would still require them to support children in need.
Temporary accommodation costs over £2bn a year would fall, but social services and NHS costs would rise. The model does not move temporary accommodation numbers for a legal change.
More families and children in unsafe accommodation or on the street, as in the period before 1977, when the statutory duty was created.

acts.title: National Minimum Wage Act 1998
acts.summary: Sets the national minimum wage (and the National Living Wage), with rates recommended by the Low Pay Commission.

knock.text: No statutory wage floor. HMRC enforcement of the minimum wage would end.
Lower wages raise Universal Credit costs and cut income tax and NICs receipts. The net fiscal effect is likely negative, but it is not modelled here.
The labour standards commitments in the Trade and Cooperation Agreement apply.
The Low Pay Commission found no significant job losses from minimum wage rises up to now, and large pay gains for the lowest paid. Repeal would reverse those gains.

acts.title: European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018
acts.summary: Repealed the European Communities Act 1972 and converted EU law into domestic law, now called assimilated law after the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023.

knock.text: Thousands of rules converted at exit (on product standards, aviation, data, the environment and employment) would lose their legal basis. This is one of the largest legal gaps a single repeal could create.
The Withdrawal Agreement, including the Windsor Framework, is given domestic effect partly through this Act. Repeal would breach the UK's obligations under the Withdrawal Agreement.
Not modelled. Trade would be disrupted at once.

acts.title: Scotland Act 1998
acts.summary: Created the Scottish Parliament and Government. Since 2016, s.63A has said they are a permanent part of the UK's constitution and will not be abolished except after a referendum in Scotland.

knock.text: Parliament is sovereign and could legally repeal the Act. But s.63A commits to a referendum first, and the Sewel convention (s.28(8)) expects the Scottish Parliament's consent.
This would be a constitutional crisis and would sharply raise support for independence.
Devolved spending of more than £50bn would return to Whitehall, along with the Barnett mechanism. Not modelled.

acts.title: Freedom of Information Act 2000
acts.summary: Gives a right of access to information held by public authorities, overseen by the Information Commissioner.

knock.text: The right to request information would end. Environmental information requests would continue under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004, which implement the Aarhus Convention.
There would be modest savings in handling time. No reliable central estimate exists.
Less public scrutiny. Several major disclosures, including the 2009 MPs' expenses scandal, began with freedom of information requests.

acts.title: Modern Slavery Act 2015
acts.summary: Consolidates slavery and trafficking offences, creates the Independent Anti-slavery Commissioner, and requires large companies to publish supply chain statements (s.54).

knock.text: The consolidated offences would go, although some older offences may revive only if the repeal says so. Victim protections would end, including the statutory defence in s.45.
The UK is party to the Council of Europe Convention on Action against Trafficking, which requires victim identification and support.

acts.title: Town and Country Planning Act 1990
acts.summary: The core of the planning system. Most development needs planning permission (s.57), decided by local planning authorities against the development plan.

amend.label: Move to zoning: permission in principle on allocated land

knock.text: Planning would become rules-based for allocated sites, as in much of Europe and the US.
More homes and higher residential investment. The model assumes private housebuilding rises 10%, at the low end of estimates for zoning reforms.
Less local say over individual schemes, and faster delivery.

acts.title: Immigration Act 1971
acts.summary: The framework for immigration control: leave to enter and remain, the right of abode, and powers of removal.

knock.text: Without a replacement there would be no statutory basis for granting or refusing leave, for border control, or for removal. Repeal on its own would not help either restrict or open migration. It would leave a legal vacuum.
Not modelled. Use the migration levers to model changes in flows.

acts.title: British Nationality Act 1981
acts.summary: Defines British citizenship and the other forms of British nationality, how they are acquired, and the limited grounds for deprivation (s.40).

knock.text: Existing citizens would keep citizenship already acquired, under Interpretation Act savings, but the rules for acquiring it, by birth, descent or naturalisation, would have no basis until replaced.

International law limits deprivation. It must not be arbitrary or discriminatory (Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 15; ICERD, Article 5) and must not leave people stateless (1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness). No change in this atlas allows deprivation of citizenship or residence by ethnicity.
Repeal would raise questions for the overseas territories and Crown dependencies, whose people's status rests on this Act.

acts.title: Welfare Reform Act 2012
acts.summary: Created Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payment (PIP) and capped household benefits.

knock.text: Universal Credit and PIP would lose their basis. Legacy benefits have mostly been closed, so this would need a replacement Act.
Not modelled as a repeal. Use the social security levers to change benefit levels.

acts.title: Homelessness Reduction Act 2017
acts.summary: Added prevention and relief duties to Part 7 of the Housing Act 1996, which apply to all eligible households and not just those in priority need.

knock.text: The prevention and relief duties would end. The main homelessness duty under the 1996 Act would remain.
Single homeless people would lose most statutory help.
